messages.author: 7d7bd1f061fa8249
messages.subject: Assessment of an EFA object
parts:
I have run an efa in lavaan using the efaUnrotate() function followed by oblqRotate(method = 'oblimin'), and I get a nice report of the usual efa type output.  But I'd like to look at some of the results a bit more thoroughly.  When I tried to use the lavaan object methods, I was told that the olbqRotate result was an EFA object, not a lavaan object.  There were only two methods of EFA objects -- 'show' and 'summary.'  I recognize that the EFA object is only a rotation of the underlying lavaan object.  Should I be looking at the underlying lavaan object for the details?  How should I be adjusting the standard errors for the rotation error and so forth? 
Thanks for the help in learning how to use lavaan.  Larry Hunsicker

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Assessment of an EFA object
parts: When I tried to use the lavaan object methods, I was told that the olbqRotate result was an EFA object, not a lavaan object

Right, so use lavaan methods on the lavaan object, which is the unrotated (but statistically equivalent) solution. e.g., you can compare the fit of 1-, 2-, 3-, and 4-factor solutions to choose a best-fitting model, etc.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Assessment of an EFA object
parts:
Thanks.  My specific problem is that I am trying compare results using efaUnrotate() with results using factanal().  I have gotten some odd results using the oblqRotate() and orthRotate() functions, and your comments seem to suggest that these are not fully vetted out functions.  But I don't know how to make the output of efaUnrotate look anything like the output of factanal, whether rotated or not (rotate = 'none').  The documentation for efaUnrotate suggests that unless one wants to "enjoy some advanced features from the lavaan package such as scaled χ^2, diagonal weighted least squares for ordinal indicators, or full-information maximum likelihood (FIML)..." the two should give similar results. I have confirmed that the cov matrix results I get from lavCor and hetcor are virtually identical.  But I don't know how to compare the results from factanal and from efaUnrotate.  When I have used psych::mixedCor and psych::fa I seem to get some very different results, and I am trying to understand why.  (I know that this is not your problem, but I can't figure out how to tell fa which of my variables are factors and which are continuous, so I have to use mixedCor and fa sequentially.)

You know that the data I am trying to analyze is largely ordered factors.  Should I be using scaled chi-square diagonal weighted least squares or FIML??  ( have been using maximum likelihood, which seems to be the default method for both factanal and efaUnrotate, and this has given me many fewer warnings and errors than psych::fa's default.

While I'm asking questions, psych::mixedCor() makes a point about the impact of a continuity correction for empty buckets in the multivariate contingency table.  I have compared using correct = "FALSE", 0.1, and 0.5, and for some of the correlations it makes a substantial difference (as stated by Revelle).  How do lavCor and hetcor handle continuity corrections?  My 13 4-valued Likert scales have 4^13 "boxes," of which it seems that about 50 are empty.  This doesn't seem to be a lot, and my sample size (460) seems large compared with many factor analyses.  But taking a log of 0 gives one a pretty big negative number.  How robust are lavCor and hetcor to empty partitions? 

Sorry to hound you with so many questions  But I hate to use a tool unless I know how it works and how I can screw it up unintentionally.  And when I get different answers using what should be parallel methods, I don't want to be choosing my answer just because I like it.  There are too many "operator degrees of freedom" to permit me to "demonstrate" something that just isn't right.

Again, thanks for your patience with me.

messages.subject: Re: Assessment of an EFA object
parts:
These are different issues as asked in the first post.

In order to help compare the results from efaUnrotate and factanal, please present the results from each one, so we can see the differences. Also, share the full call you are making for the functions

If you have ordered variables, you should use the WLS estimators, that can be use in efaUnrotate, and evaluate the scales chi-square and fit indices. Using FIML would assume the items are continuous, this may be a reason for the difference in results.

Also, be sure of using the same rotation method for both methods when comparing

messages.subject: Re: Assessment of an EFA object
parts:
As far as I can see in the psych::fa information page, it assumes all variables are continuous. This by definition will provide different results

I dont knwo what you mean by "that orth and oblq Rotate functions were not fully vetted", the rotate functions dont the rotation, but call GPArotation package which provides the standard for the different rotation methods.

I think you are misunderstanding how semTools handles the EFA methods. The result from efaUnrotate is a lavaan object, so when you look at the model fit you ask it from this object as fitMeasures(), which you can also look at the unrotated factor loadings with summary(). But this are not interpretable because they EFA factor loadings need to be rotated. Then you use one of the rotation methods you have interpretable factor loadings and factor correlations. 

Now, from the rotated result you showed, first orthogonal rotations are not recomended, because it is hard to argue that the factors are not correlated. Second, are you confident that the 5 factor solution is a "good" solution based on model fit?. Third, given those factor loadings, with only 1 item having a factor loading higher than 0.3 for factor 4, and that one having an out of bounds value as -205, I would disregard that as a bad factor solution.

Also, you should consider the number of factors in function of the number of items. So, in an EFA every item has a factor loading to every factor, so if you have "too many" factors in function of the number of items will be more likely to have "weird" results.

I havent seen clear rules on how many factors in relation with the number of items. The relation I follow is in function  to have 3 items per factor, so in your case 16/3 = 5.3. I would recommend to proceed with caution around 5 factors and above in this data

I would recommend an analysis workflow like this




library(semTools)


### run EFA for number of factors from 1 to 8
efa_res <- list(nf1 = efaUnrotate(csbx1[-14], nf=1, missing = 'pairwise', estimator="wlsmv"),
                nf2 = efaUnrotate(csbx1[-14], nf=2, missing = 'pairwise', estimator="wlsmv"),
                nf3 = efaUnrotate(csbx1[-14], nf=3, missing = 'pairwise', estimator="wlsmv"),
                nf4 = efaUnrotate(csbx1[-14], nf=4, missing = 'pairwise', estimator="wlsmv"),
                nf5 = efaUnrotate(csbx1[-14], nf=5, missing = 'pairwise', estimator="wlsmv"),
                nf6 = efaUnrotate(csbx1[-14], nf=6, missing = 'pairwise', estimator="wlsmv"),
                nf7 = efaUnrotate(csbx1[-14], nf=7, missing = 'pairwise', estimator="wlsmv"),
                nf8 = efaUnrotate(csbx1[-14], nf=8, missing = 'pairwise', estimator="wlsmv"))


### function to extract summary fit indices
fit_efas <- function(object){
  fit_ind <- c(fitMeasures(object)[c("chisq.scaled","df.scaled","pvalue.scaled","cfi.scaled","rmsea.scaled","rmsea.ci.lower.scaled","rmsea.ci.upper.scaled","srmr")],
               moreFitIndices(fit, fit.measures = "gammaHat.scaled"))
  return(fit_ind)
}



t(sapply(efa_res, fit_efas))
### pick 2 or 3 number of factors that do fit well enough,
### and look at the rotated soultions for interpretability
### for example:


reas_rotated <- list(oblqRotate(efa_res[[4]],method = "quartimin"),
                     oblqRotate(efa_res[[5]],method = "quartimin"))


### look at which solution if more interpretable
### rotated solution for 4 factors
summary(reas_rotated[[1]], sort = FALSE, suppress = 0.3)

On Thursday, December 5, 2019 at 1:57:52 PM UTC-6, Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal wrote:
Also, you should consider the number of factors in function of the number of items. So, in an EFA every item has a factor loading to every factor, so if you have "too many" factors in function of the number of items will be more likely to have "weird" results.

I havent seen clear rules on how many factors in relation with the number of items. The relation I follow is in function  to have 3 items per factor, so in your case 16/3 = 5.3. I would recommend to proceed with caution around 5 factors and above in this data



On Thursday, December 5, 2019 at 1:35:02 PM UTC-6, Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal wrote:


As far as I can see in the psych::fa information page, it assumes all variables are continuous. This by definition will provide different results

I dont knwo what you mean by "that orth and oblq Rotate functions were not fully vetted", the rotate functions dont the rotation, but call GPArotation package which provides the standard for the different rotation methods.

I think you are misunderstanding how semTools handles the EFA methods. The result from efaUnrotate is a lavaan object, so when you look at the model fit you ask it from this object as fitMeasures(), which you can also look at the unrotated factor loadings with summary(). But this are not interpretable because they EFA factor loadings need to be rotated. Then you use one of the rotation methods you have interpretable factor loadings and factor correlations. 

Now, from the rotated result you showed, first orthogonal rotations are not recomended, because it is hard to argue that the factors are not correlated. Second, are you confident that the 5 factor solution is a "good" solution based on model fit?. Third, given those factor loadings, with only 1 item having a factor loading higher than 0.3 for factor 4, and that one having an out of bounds value as -205, I would disregard that as a bad factor solution.
